title: What is known about 1RB1LB_1LC0RD_0LE1LA_0RF1RA_1LE0LA_---0RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LB_1LC0RD_0LE1LA_0RF1RA_1LE0LA_---0RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. On single cells one round trip is a cellular automaton: c'[p] = 1 xor c[p] xor c[p+3] from the left end to the first 00, proved in Lean for every tape with no lone 1 before that point (lean/Trip.lean), walls included; with lone 1s it is the same automaton on the tape with their holes filled, and the machine halts exactly when such a hole chain meets a 0 (lean/Token.lean). So the tape is three interleaved copies of rule 102 and the only thing that can go wrong is a lone 1 before the turn (token mode). A fast simulator built on this reaches 5.2·1013 steps with no halt and no lone 1 after 8.5·106 steps. Earlier results: The sweep rule is proved: writing x = 111 and y = 110, one round trip of the head replaces each word by the XOR of it and its right neighbour (rule 102), in Lean for every length, with its Lucas closed form. A halt needs a 10 defect with y in front of it and only ys up to the next wall. Lean now proves what a deep sweep does at a defect: with x in front it is rule 102 on the whole line, with y in front the defect jumps to the end of the gap's first x block, and after a jump over m slots the next jump comes exactly m sweeps later. So a defect's whole life is one map on its gap, and the danger pattern is a jump with nothing to land on. Lean also proves which gaps can get there: under shielded sweeps exactly the rows of Pascal's triangle mod 2, and at the next jump exactly one rest C for each jump length L (word k is y iff k and L share no binary 1). The map does not rule that out by itself; a proof also needs to show that no new bulk 10 defect is born, which in the run has not happened since 8.5 million steps. No closed tape language has been found.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: B with 1 under the head, 0 right, 0 two right. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 43,577 cells have been visited and 35,099 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.067).

claims.title: Shift rules over 3-cell words
claims.text: Ten rules, each for every n and every surrounding tape: for example D turns (101)<sup>n</sup> into (110)<sup>n</sup> going right, B turns (110)<sup>n</sup> into (011)<sup>n</sup>, A runs left over (110)<sup>n</sup> turning it into (111)<sup>n</sup>.

claims.title: One round trip is rule 102, for every length
claims.text: For every word string w ending in y and followed by a 0, started in B on its first cell: the right sweep turns x into 000 and y into 011, B on the 0 writes 1 and turns, and the left sweep (C or E remembering the word to the right) writes back word i as w[i] xor w[i+1], with y after the end. The last word becomes x and the 0 after the string a 1.

claims.title: One round trip is a cellular automaton on cells
claims.text: From the head on a new leftmost (blank) cell in A, with runs of at least two 1s each followed by one 0 up to a second 0 (that is, no lone 1 before the first 00): the cells from the start cell to the first 0 of the pair become c[p] == c[p+3] (= 1 xor c[p] xor c[p+3]) with 1 1 0 imagined after them, the second 0 becomes 1, nothing further right is read, and the head ends one cell left, in A, after 4(Q − lo) − 6z + 15 steps. The left sweep spends one step per cell, its state naming the three original cells to its right. This covers every round trip without token mode, walls included; the word rule of Xor.lean is the special case of clean words.

claims.title: Where a lone 1 can come from
claims.text: If no three neighbouring cells hold two 0s, the automaton writes 0 1 0 at p, p+1, p+2 only when the cells p … p+5 were 0 1 1 1 1 0. A lone 1 before the turn is the only thing a round trip cannot cross (token mode, where the halt lives).

claims.title: Token mode is the same automaton on the filled tape
claims.text: Over a lone 1 followed by j words 110 and a 111, the right sweep leaves exactly the cells and state it would leave over the tape with those holes filled. So every round trip over ordinary runs and token chains is the cell automaton on the filled tape, which differs from the plain automaton at exactly two cells (the defect's jump); if the 110 words run into a 0 the machine halts. py/trip_model.py reproduces all 10,528 round trips of the first 6·107 steps with this map.

claims.title: No halt in 5.2·10<sup>13</sup> steps, no lone 1 after 8.5·10<sup>6</sup>
claims.text: c/trips.c does each round trip that trip covers with 64-bit word operations and runs every other trip (token mode, the trips that reach the right end) on the machine's table. 107 round trips, 52,496,781,276,447 steps: no halt; the 18 trips with a lone 1 before the turn all come before 8.5·106 steps. In checking mode it also runs every trip on the machine and compares the whole tape and the step count (3·105 trips, no difference).

claims.title: How a bulk 10 is born, in cells
claims.text: Between two walls the 0s of one copy of rule 102 are multiplied by (1 + u) at each pass (u = three cells left), so after a plain pass their number is even, and a turn at either wall deletes one. A bulk 10 is born when a segment's 0s run out at a turn at its left wall; that needs, first, a trip whose turn ends a segment of y words only (0s every three cells) with a 111 wall on its left. The run has 5 such trips (at 92, 108, 1,904, 2,608 and 3,403 round trips); each is followed by the token-mode trips of one 10 lifetime, and there is none in the next 106 trips. The y-only segments that keep forming sit 10, 17, 24 and 53 cells from the right end, behind walls of 6, 9 or 18 cells, as part of the right end's periodic cycle.

claims.title: Many round trips: Lucas' theorem
claims.text: Iterating rule 102 with a fixed word after the end, word i after t sweeps is the XOR of the starting words i + k over the k ≤ t with C(t, k) odd, i.e. the binary digits of k and t − k disjoint. For a gap of n x's next to the fixed y, word j from the y is y iff C(t, j) is odd, so the whole gap is y first after 2b − 1 sweeps, 2b > n.

claims.title: The danger pattern halts; an x in front shields the defect
claims.text: B at the start of y 10 yn 0 halts for every n: the defect puts B in token mode, F crosses the y words turning each into 000, and F reads the wall's 0. With x before the defect, x 10 is the single run 11110, which B rewrites to 00011 and leaves at the start of the gap the ordinary way.

claims.title: The defect's two deep sweeps: shielded, or a jump
claims.text: For all word strings and lengths. Shielded (x before the defect T): P x T G y 0 becomes x102(P, x) T x102(y G y, y) 1, the defect one slot further left; counting T as a y this is rule 102 on the whole line (x102_shielded). Jump (y before T): P y T yj xa+1 C y 0, with C empty or starting with y, becomes x102(P y, x) xj+a+1 T x102(C y, y) 1: the defect jumps to the last slot of the gap's first x block. With no x before the wall this is the danger pattern, which halts.

claims.title: The jump clock
claims.text: After a jump over m = j + a + 1 slots the words before the defect are Q y xm; each shielded sweep turns Q y xk into Q' y xk−1. So exactly m shielded sweeps follow and then the word before the defect is y again: the next jump (or merge, or the danger pattern) comes m sweeps later, whatever the words further left.

claims.title: The deep-sweep rules, against the machine's table
claims.text: The shielded rule for every P of up to 5 words and G of up to 6 (8,001 cases), the jump for P up to 5 words, j up to 4, a + 1 up to 4 and C up to 5 words (40,320 cases), and the danger pattern (504 cases, all halt), run with the machine's own table.

claims.title: A defect's lifetime is one map on the gap
claims.text: Read the gap with the defect as constant term, W = 1 + g0 z + … over GF(2). Shielded sweeps multiply W by 1 + z; a jump strips the leading run of ones and the run of zeros after it (L = j + a + 2 slots) and, with the clock, gives F(W) = (1 + z)L C at the next jump. The left words fix only the first jump. Every deep sweep of the real run to 1.2·107 steps (54 shielded, 10 jumps, 3 merges) follows the rules, the gap agrees with the model on every word the old gap determines (63 of 63), and all 10 jumps and merges after a first jump came on the clock. For random gaps the run of ones at a jump is geometric (py/fmap.py), so the map does not by itself prevent a halt; the real run had j = 0 or 1 at every jump.

claims.title: Which gaps shielded sweeps can turn all y: Pascal rows
claims.text: Read the gap with the defect as constant term, W = 1 + g0 z + … over GF(2). t shielded sweeps multiply it by (1 + z)t, and the first r coefficients of the result are all y iff they were those of mask t, the series whose coefficient k is 1 exactly when k and t share no binary 1 (it is (1 + z)−(t+1); Pascal's rule is the whole proof). mask has period 2b below 2b, so a gap of fewer than 2b words ever becomes all y iff it is one of the 2b series mask t, t < 2b: the rows of Pascal's triangle mod 2 found earlier (checked before in py/pascal_gaps.py for every gap up to 14 words), now proved for all lengths. The Lean file also proves that the shielded sweep of Hop.lean is multiplication by 1 + z on every coefficient the old gap determines (ser_shielded).

claims.title: Which gaps a jump can make dangerous
claims.text: At a jump over yj xa+1 with rest C (L = j + a + 2), the series at the next jump is F(W) = (1 + z)L C, and its first r coefficients are all y iff C agrees with mask L on its first r words: word k of C must be y exactly when k and L share no binary 1. So the run of y words at the next jump is one less than the length of the common prefix of C and mask L, and the danger pattern at the next jump (the run reaches the wall) needs C = mask L on every word: for each (j, a) exactly one gap, so at most about n2/2 of the 2n gaps of n words (190 of 1,048,576 for n = 20). ser_jump ties this to the words of jump in Hop.lean: the gap it leaves is (1 + z) C on every coefficient the old gap determines.

claims.title: The next-jump rule, against the real run
claims.text: py/jump_gaps.py checks the agreement rule on 163,800 cases (every C of up to 12 words, L up to 40) and reads the real run to 1.2·107 steps: at all 10 jumps that have a successor in the same lifetime, the run at the next jump is the agreement with mask L minus one. The closest calls are at 2.53·106 steps, where C = yyxx is mask 6 on every word the old gap holds (the next run is 3 and the gap had grown to 7, so the words that entered at the wall decided it), and at 5.44·106 steps (agreement 4 of 5, run 3 where 4 would have halted). So the jump map pins down the dangerous gaps exactly, but the words fed in at the wall between jumps are not yet controlled.

claims.title: A 10 defect is a pinned y in a rule-102 line
claims.text: In the run to 9·106 steps, every sweep with an x before a bulk 10 defect (50 of them) moves the words on both sides by w'[i] = w[i−1] xor w[i] in the defect's frame, with the defect acting as a fixed y for the gap. So the word before the defect is a Lucas sum of the words left of it (checked for 36 sweeps). The other 9 sweeps are exactly those with y before the defect: the defect jumps (see the jump rule above). A halt needs such a sweep to meet an all-y gap; the two never coincided.

claims.title: The string is rewritten every sweep
claims.text: At successive visits of the head to the left end (steps 2,918,884 … 2,994,219) the left string is different each time, not shifted copies of one another, and the visited width grows by one or two cells per visit (2,366 → 2,395 in 29 visits). Read as words of 3 cells it is a string over 110 and 111.

claims.title: Regular-language deciders tried (F11)
claims.text: None of these closes: each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction, which says nothing about whether the machine halts. n-gram CPS (tools/c/ngramcps.c), equal widths on both sides: a halting local configuration is reached with plain up to width 15, history 1 up to width 20, history 2 up to width 20, history 3 up to width 20, LRU history up to width 6 (larger widths ran out of the 150 s or 60 million configuration budget). n-gram CPS with every cell tagged by its position mod p: fails for p = 2 up to width 16, p = 3 up to width 16, p = 4 up to width 16, p = 6 up to width 16. n-gram CPS where each side also carries the state of a small automaton that has read that side from the far end (every automaton with up to 3 states on both sides, or 4 states on one side), with position mod 1..4 and widths 4, 6, 8: no closed set without a halt in all 120 parameter sets. Run-length windows (the K nearest runs of equal macro cells on each side, run lengths kept exactly below T and mod M above): fails for all 72 parameter sets (cells of 1 to 4 bits, K = 2, 4, 6, T = 2, 4, M = 1, 2, 4). Two-automaton closed tape language by SAT (a deterministic automaton reading each side inward, n states each, CaDiCaL): no solution for n = 2..8; n = 9 not finished in 150 s.
claims.where: sweeps of 13 November 2026 (family F11); the tagged and run-length deciders are not in the repository yet

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Open: the transformation the sweep performs on the string (presumably arithmetic on the number it encodes) is not identified.

claims.title: One sweep pair is the XOR rule
claims.text: Write x = 111 and y = 110. For every word string w over {x, y} ending in y, up to 16 words (65,535 strings): started in B on its first cell the machine sweeps right without turning, rewriting each run 1<sup>m</sup>0 as 0<sup>m−1</sup>11; started in C at the end of that it sweeps left without turning; the result is the word string v with v<sub>i</sub> = w<sub>i</sub> xor w<sub>i+1</sub> (x = 0, y = 1), last word x. This is the linear rule 102 cellular automaton, so every word string can occur and the left string looks random.
claims.where: py/xor_epoch.py, exhaustive per length, run with the machine's own table

claims.title: Defects are walls emitted at the right end
claims.text: Where the word alignment shifts (a run of 1s of length 0 or 1 mod 3, or a double 0) there is a wall between two XOR domains. A single wall survives each epoch and cycles z2 → 13k → 13k−3 → … → 13 → z2, drifting left. A right sweep stops at the first double-0 wall (B reads 0), so walls act like digits of a counter. Walls are created by a 5-phase cycle at the right end, which grows by 2 cells per cycle. A halt needs the token parser (state B) at 1 0 0: a single 1 (seen only within about 30 runs of the right end) followed by 110 words and then a double 0; it was not seen in 3·108 steps.

claims.title: Closed tape language searches (16 November 2026)
claims.text: None closes; each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction or runs out of budget. Abstract regular model checking over whole-tape automata, merging states by k-step Moore equivalence (forward, reversed, both), k = 1..6, forward from blank and backward from F reading 0. Run-length windows with lengths mod 3 (the F11 sweep tried M = 1, 2, 4 only): K = 2..16 nearest runs with exact lengths below 3 halt; exact lengths up to 4..8, or runs near the blank ends kept exact, exceed 5 to 30 million abstract configurations. The reason found: the bulk is a full shift (any word string), so windows of K runs grow like 2<sup>K</sup>, while the right end needs exact lengths.
claims.where: c/rlwin.cpp (run-length windows); the model-checking scripts are in the project folder ctl-696/tools

claims.title: Halting needs a short gap that the XOR rule turns all y
claims.text: Every left-visit tape up to 3·107 steps parses as words 111 and 110 with inserted defects 0 and 10. The halting read 1 0 0 needs the pattern 0 10 (110)* 0, which never occurs. In mutation tests on real tapes, random words between defects stay clear in 99 of 100 runs over 60 more left visits; every halting run, shrunk to its smallest change, alters the words W in a gap 10 W 0, which the XOR rule then turns into all 110 (for example 10 xyxyx 0 becomes 10 yyyyy 0), giving the pattern. So what keeps the machine from halting is a condition on the XOR orbit of these gaps, of any length, which a fixed-window closed tape language cannot express.

claims.title: No new 10 defect after 8.5 million steps
claims.text: Reading the defects as particles with charge mod 3 (0 = 1, 10 = 2): a 10 in the bulk forms when two 0 walls with only 111 words between them meet and the word before the left wall is 110 (110 0 111…111 0; with 111 before the wall, such gaps are common and never merge), and it ends by cancelling with the next 0 wall. In the real run there are only four such lifetimes, the last ending at 8.5·106 steps, and none forms after that up to 1011 steps (21,812 tapes checked, no halt). While one lives, the words after it change by vi = wi−1 xor wi with 110 fed in from the left. They became all 110 131 times, and each time the word before the 10 was 111, so the halting pattern never formed. The trigger 110 0 111…111 0 was last seen at 4.07·106 steps in the same census.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The left half of the tape is a long string of two 3-cell words, x = 111 and y = 110, and each round trip of the head replaces every word by the XOR of it and its right neighbour: a linear cellular automaton running on the tape. What could make it halt is a defect coming in from the right end.

facts.text: No halt (round trips done by the proved cell rule, the rest on the machine).
One round trip, for every tape with no lone 1 before its first 00.
One round trip on the words 111 = 0, 110 = 1 (every string up to 16 words).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.067).
After 109 steps the tape spans 43,577 cells (31,721 left of the start, 197 right), with a density of 1s of 0.805.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A string of 110s and 111s, run by the XOR rule
html: At step 985,607,083 the head is at the left end and the tape starts A>0 0 1^6 0 1^8 0 1^2 0 1^5 0 1^2 0 1^5 0 1^2 0 1^2 0 1^2 0 1^14 …: runs of 1s whose lengths are 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, … (2 more than a multiple of 3) separated by single 0s. In 3-cell words that is a string over x = 111 and y = 110, about 10,000 words long.

The rule. From the left end the head sweeps right in state B, reading one run at a time: 1^m 0 becomes 0^(m-1) 1 1 (the zigzag B→D→A→B moves one cell right every three steps). At the right it turns and sweeps left in states E, A, B, C, which turns the 0-runs back into 1-runs. Put together, word i of the new string is x if words i and i+1 of the old string were equal and y if they differed:

words
beforey y x y x x x x y y
afterx y y y x x x y x …

With x = 0 and y = 1 that is vi = wi xor wi+1, the linear cellular automaton called rule 102, whose pictures are Sierpinski triangles. py/xor_epoch.py checks it with the machine's own table for every string of up to 16 words. So the string is not a number in some base: it is a linear automaton, and any word string can appear.

Walls. Where the 3-cell alignment shifts (a run of length 0 or 1 mod 3, or a double 0) two XOR domains meet. A single wall survives: it cycles 00 → 1^(3k) → 1^(3k-3) → … → 1^3 → 00 while drifting left. A right sweep stops at the first 00 wall, so the walls behave like the digits of a counter, and the small structure at the right end (a 5-phase cycle that gains 2 cells per cycle) is where new walls come from.

sections.heading: One round trip is a cellular automaton on cells
html: Forget the words for a moment and look at single cells. A round trip starts when the head first stands on a new cell at the left end. Let Q be the first place where two 0s stand side by side. If no 1 stands alone (0 1 0) before Q, the whole round trip is one line:
c'[p] = 1 xor c[p] xor c[p+3]   for every cell p from the left end to Q

with three imagined cells 1 1 0 after Q. The second 0 of the pair becomes a 1, nothing further right is read, and the head ends one cell further left. Lean proves this for every such tape (trip in lean/Trip.lean), with the exact number of steps, 4(Q − lo) − 6z + 15, where z counts the 0s. The proof is short because the way back is a machine that spends exactly one step on each cell: its state names the three cells to its right as they were before the trip (E = 111, C = 110, B = 101, A = 011), and it writes c[p] == c[p+3].

So the machine is three interleaved copies of rule 102: cells p, p+3, p+6, … form one copy, and a 0 only ever spreads to p − 3. In the word picture one copy carries the data and the other two sit at 1; a wall is a place where the data passes to the next copy. The rule does not see walls at all. The only thing a round trip cannot cross is a lone 1, and Lean also proves where that comes from: in a tape where no three neighbouring cells hold two 0s, a lone 1 at p+1 appears only from 0 1 1 1 1 0 at p … p+5 (iso_birth).

The machine runs from a blank tape in your browser. For the round trip you pick, the first row is the tape when the trip starts, the second is what the formula predicts, and the third is what the machine's own table actually leaves. 0s are coloured by their cell number mod 3, which is the copy of rule 102 they belong to. The orange outline marks the pair of 0s where the head turns.

Three copies of rule 102 in the real run

One row per round trip (every 8th one for the right end, which changes slowly), time going down, every cell drawn: 1s light, 0s coloured by cell number mod 3. A 0 spreads only three cells to the left, so each colour draws its own Pascal triangle. Where one colour hands over to the next there is a wall. At the left end the triangles of the newest data; at the right end the walls come in and count down.

What this changes for the halting question. A trip can only go wrong where a 1 stands alone before the first 00, which is the token mode of the right sweep. In the run that happens in 18 trips, all before 8.5·106 steps. A fast simulator built on the trip rule (c/trips.c: the trips the rule covers are done 64 cells at a time, every other trip is run on the machine's table) reaches 5.2·1013 steps with no halt and no further lone 1. Run with checking switched on, it compares the whole tape with the machine after every trip and finds no difference.

The rule also answers the wall-words question exactly. Between two walls the 0s of one copy are multiplied by (1 + u) at each pass (u = three cells to the left), so after a plain pass their number is even. A turn at either wall deletes one 0. A new 10 defect is born exactly when the 0s of a segment run out at a turn, and that needs a segment of y words only (0s every three cells), ending at the turn, with a 111 wall to its left. The run has five such trips. Each was followed by token-mode trips, which are the four lifetimes of a bulk 10 and one early one, and none comes after 8.5·106 steps. The y-only segments that do keep forming sit 10, 17, 24 and 53 cells from the right end, behind walls of 6, 9 and 18 cells, in the right end's periodic cycle.

sections.heading: Rule 102 in Lean, and which gaps are dangerous
html:
One round trip is rule 102, for every length (Lean, epoch in lean/Xor.lean). Read the left side as words x = 111 (bit 0) and y = 110 (bit 1). Start in B on the first cell of a word string that ends in y, with a 0 after it. The right sweep turns each x into 000 and each y into 011 (B zigzags: B 1 1 → 0 B 1). B on the 0 writes a 1 and turns. The left sweep remembers one bit, C when the word to its right was y and E when it was x, and writes back the XOR of each word and its right neighbour. For every word string, not only the 65,535 checked before.

Many round trips, by Lucas' theorem (Lean, closed_form and allx in lean/XorLucas.lean). After t round trips with a fixed word at the end, word i is the XOR of the starting words i + k over the k whose binary digits lie inside those of t. For a gap of xs next to a fixed y, word j (counted from the y) is y exactly when the digits of j lie inside those of t.

The danger pattern, in binary digits. A halt needs a 10 defect whose gap 10 W 0 has become all y, with a y or 0 in front of the defect. In the gap the defect side acts as a fixed y. Over GF(2) one sweep multiplies the gap polynomial by 1 + z, and all y is (1 + z)2b − 1 (with 2b above the gap length). So a gap ever becomes all y exactly when it already is a row of Pascal's triangle mod 2, and then at the sweeps t ≡ 2b − 1 − s (mod 2b), where s is the row. Only 2b ≤ 2n of the 2n gaps of length n can do it (proved in Lean for every length: reach_ones and pascal_reach in lean/Gaps.lean). Type a gap below, with the defect on the left.

Row t is the gap after t sweeps; the first column is the fixed y of the defect, dark is y. Rows where the whole gap is y are marked on the right. The pattern repeats after 2b rows.

sections.heading: Where a 10 defect goes when a y stands in front of it
html: The jump, in Lean (lean/Hop.lean). A deep sweep reaches a bulk 10 defect T and turns at the wall after its gap. With x in front (shielded), P x T G y 0 becomes x102(P, x) T x102(y G y, y) 1: the defect moves one slot left, and counting T as a y the whole line is one row of rule 102. With y in front (jump), P y T yj xa+1 C y 0 becomes x102(P y, x) xj+a+1 T x102(C y, y) 1: the right sweep crosses the ys in token mode, the first x throws it back into ordinary mode one cell late, and the defect jumps forward to the last slot of the gap's first x block. With no x before the wall there is nowhere to land, and that is the danger pattern, which halts. If the first x block runs into the wall, defect and wall cancel.

The clock (clock). After a jump over m = j + a + 1 slots the words before T are … y xm, so exactly m shielded sweeps follow and then a y stands before T again: the next jump comes m sweeps later, whatever the words further left. In the real run to 1.2·107 steps all 54 shielded sweeps, 10 jumps and 3 merges follow these rules, and all 10 jumps and merges after a first jump came on the clock (py/defect_life.py).

One map for a whole lifetime. Write the gap with T as the constant term, W = 1 + g0 z + g1 z2 + … over GF(2). A shielded sweep multiplies W by 1 + z. A jump strips the leading run of ones and the run of zeros after it (L slots) and keeps (1 + z) C of the rest C. With the clock, jump to jump is F(W) = (1 + z)L C. The words left of the defect matter only once, for the first jump (the first sweep where their Lucas sum is y). It halts when, at a jump, the run of ones reaches the wall. For random gaps that run is as long as a run of coin flips (py/fmap.py), so the map alone does not prevent a halt; what has kept the real run safe is which gaps were born, and no bulk 10 has been born since 8.5·106 steps.

Which gaps a jump can make dangerous (Lean, next_jump_run in lean/Gaps.lean). Undoing (1 + z)L is multiplying by (1 + z)−L, and (1 + z)−(L+1) has coefficient k equal to C(L + k, k) mod 2, which by Lucas is 1 exactly when k and L share no binary 1. Call that series mask L. Then the run of ys at the next jump is one less than the number of leading words on which the rest C agrees with mask L. A halt at the next jump needs C = mask L on the whole gap: one gap for each jump length, out of 2n. In the real run the rule held at all 10 jumps; the closest call (2.53·106 steps) had C equal to mask 6 on every word the old gap held, and the words that came in at the wall between jumps broke the run. sections.heading: From cells to walls, interactively
html: The same tape can be read at five levels, each one coarser than the last and each one following from the one below it:
• Cells. 0s and 1s and a head in one of six states: the machine itself.
• Runs. Going right in state B, the head reads one run 1^m 0 at a time and writes 0^(m-1) 1 1. Going left in states E, A, B, C it turns the 0-runs back into 1-runs.
• Words. Runs of 1s have length 2, 5, 8, … so the tape cuts into 3-cell words, x = 111 and y = 110.
• Bits and the XOR rule. With x = 0 and y = 1, one round trip of the head turns bit i into (bit i) xor (bit i+1). That is the linear cellular automaton rule 102.

• Domains and walls. Where the 3-cell cut shifts by one or two cells, two XOR domains meet at a wall. Walls come in from the right end and drift left. A halt would need a wall in one particular shape.
The ladder: one real tape at every level

The machine runs from a blank tape in your browser. The tape is taken each time the head reaches a new cell at the left end, which is the start of a round trip. Pick a moment and a window; each row below reads the same cells one level up.
wall (a run that breaks the 3-cell cut)
domain, coloured by where its words start (cell number mod 3)
Levels 1 to 4: run the machine on any word string

Type a string of x and y. Right sweep starts the real machine in state B on the first cell and runs it until it steps past the end. Left sweep then starts it in state C on the last cell and runs it until it leaves the left end. Each sweep is the machine's own table, step by step, with nothing shortcut. The last line compares the result with the XOR rule. A final y is kept at the right end, so the string keeps its length.
Level 4: many round trips draw a Sierpinski triangle

Each row is one round trip of the machine (computed by the real table, as above) on the row above it, drawn as bits: y is dark and x is light. Bit i of the next row depends only on bits i and i+1, so a pattern spreads only to the left and every triangle is right-angled, with its corner at the top right: half of the familiar Sierpinski triangle, nothing is cut off. The y held at the right end (drawn as an extra column at the right edge, always dark) feeds the pattern, which is why the last real column alternates: it is that column xor y. Starting from all x gives one clean triangle; at 32, 64, 128 or 256 words it exactly fills the square. The XOR rule predicts every pixel, and the counter confirms that the machine agrees.
Level 5: domains and walls in the real run

One row per round trip of the real run from a blank tape, with time going down and the left end growing to the left. Each cell is coloured by its domain, that is where its 3-cell words start (cell number mod 3). Walls are drawn in orange. Each single wall cycles 00 → 1^(3k) → 1^(3k-3) → … → 1^3 → 00 as it drifts left. A right sweep stops at the first 00 wall, so the walls behave like the digits of a counter. New walls appear at the right end. Switch to bits and the last 400 to see the XOR rule in the real run: on the left, which is updated on every round trip, the tape is the random-looking rule 102 texture, full of right-angled triangles. Behind each 00 wall the bits stand still (vertical stripes) until a sweep gets past it.

sections.heading: Open
html: The only halt is F reading 0. It needs the right sweep's token reader (state B) to stand on 1 0 0: a run of a single 1, possibly followed by several 110 words read one cell out of step, running into a double-0 wall. Single 1s occur only within about 30 runs of the right end, and this combination was never seen in 3·108 steps.

A closed tape language (a regular set of tapes that contains the start, is closed under a step and has no halt) would settle it, and was searched for on 16 November 2026 with whole-tape automata and with run-length windows that count lengths mod 3; none closed. The bulk can hold any word string, so local windows explode, while the walls near the right end need exact lengths. A language that keeps the right end exact and lets the bulk be any word string with walls is the next thing to try.

summary: On single cells one round trip is the cellular automaton c'[p] = 1 xor c[p] xor c[p+3] up to the first 00 (proved in Lean for every tape without a lone 1 there): three interleaved copies of rule 102, the words 111/110 being one of them. A halt needs a lone 1 before the turn; none after 8.5 million steps, no halt in 5.2·10^13 steps.
